record.paper_title: On a general Syracuse problem with conjectures
record.context_brief: Classical Collatz conjecture in Syracuse-map notation
record.original_question: For the classical Collatz/Syracuse map T(n)=n/2 when n is even and T(n)=(3n+1)/2 when n is odd, is Ω(1)=(1→2→1) the only cycle, and does every positive integer eventually reach 1, so that N=G(1) and there are no divergent trajectories G(∞)=∅?

evidence.quote: The well-known conjecture of the 3 x+1 problem (or Collatz’s conjecture ) states that, for any initial value n ∈ N, there is a positive integer k ∈ N0 such that S(k)(n) = 1. A second conjecture in the Syracuse problem states that the trivial c ycle (1 → 2 → 1) is the unique cycle in the graph associated to the map S.

Conjecture 2.2. (Collatz conjecture) For the parameters a = 3 and b = 1 the set C(3, 1) contains only one cycle (the trivial one): C(3, 1) = { Ω(1)} , with Ω(1) = (1 → 2 → 1) and we have: N = G(1) and G(∞ ) = ∅ .

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Define the Syracuse map $T:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ on the positive integers by
$$T(n)=\begin{cases} n/2, & n\equiv 0\pmod 2,\\ (3n+1)/2, & n\equiv 1\pmod 2.\end{cases}$$
For $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $k\in\mathbb{N}_0$, let $T^{(k)}$ denote the $k$-fold iterate of $T$, with $T^{(0)}(n)=n$. A cycle of $T$ is a finite sequence $(n_0\to n_1\to\cdots\to n_{\ell-1}\to n_0)$ with $n_{i+1}=T(n_i)$ and all $n_i$ distinct; the trivial cycle is $\Omega(1)=(1\to 2\to 1)$. Let $G(1)=\{n\in\mathbb{N}:\exists k\in\mathbb{N}_0,\ T^{(k)}(n)=1\}$ and let $G(\infty)=\{n\in\mathbb{N}: T^{(k)}(n)\to\infty\text{ as }k\to\infty\}$.

Prove or disprove the following two statements:
(a) The trivial cycle $\Omega(1)=(1\to 2\to 1)$ is the unique cycle of $T$ in $\mathbb{N}$.
(b) $G(1)=\mathbb{N}$ and $G(\infty)=\varnothing$; equivalently, for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ there exists $k\in\mathbb{N}_0$ with $T^{(k)}(n)=1$.
artifact.status_search_result: The statement is the classical Collatz (3x+1) conjecture, which remains open. Partial progress includes Tao's 2019/2022 result that almost all orbits attain almost bounded values, but the full conjecture is unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Almost all orbits of the Collatz map attain almost bounded values
status_evidence.snippet: Tao proves that almost all Collatz orbits attain almost bounded values, while the full Collatz conjecture remains open.
status_evidence.claim: The Collatz conjecture is still open; only partial/density results are known.
